newsitem.title: USA: Fed increasingly likely to raise rates - sources.
newsitem.headline: Fed increasingly likely to raise rates - sources.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve looks increasingly likely to raise interest rates soon to rein in the surging economy and head off incipient inflation, central bank sources said on Friday.
The move -- which would be the Fed's first increase in about 1-1/2 years -- could come this month and would likely be on the order of a quarter percentage point, not the half feared by Wall Street.

The sources, who declined to be identified, said a short-term rate increase was not a "done deal," but added that the odds of one occuring has gone up as the economy has shown scant signs of slowing from its hectic second quarter pace.
"There's increasingly less to argue about (when it comes to deciding whether to raise rates)," one source said.

The latest indication of the economy's overall strength came on Friday with news that the unemployment rate fell to 5.1 percent in August, its lowest level in nearly 7-1/2 years, as the economy created 250,000 jobs.
The central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee holds its next meeting on September 24.
Fed policymakers have been divided for several months over whether a rate hike is needed to keep a cap on inflation.
"Depending on who you talk to, you can get some very different views," one central bank source said.

Anti-inflation hawks, led by several of the regional Fed bank presidents, have argued that the central bank may have already fallen behind in the battle against inflation and that a rate rise of as much as a half point was needed.
But the so-called doves, including some of President Clinton's appointees to the Fed board here in Washington, have resisted calls for higher rates because inflation has been quiescent.

"The question is when does the whole center of the group shift," one central bank source said. "At what point does (Fed chairman) Alan Greenspan exercise some leadership and say this is what needs to be done."

Several Fed sources suggested that day may be drawing nearer. In his "Humphrey-Hawkins" testimony to Congress in July, Greenspan voiced hopes that the economic growth would moderate from its rapid 4.8-percent annualized rate in the second quarter so as to keep inflation in check.
That has not happened, at least so far.
"It's hard to see a whole lot of softness (in the economy)," one Fed source said, adding, "The long-awaited slowdown may be in the works, but it's not evident."
Home and automobile sales have held up, despite a rise in long-term interest rates. Consumer confidence is at a six-year high and the labor market has been strong.
And companies seem to be stepping up production, in part to rebuild depleted inventories.
The economy's continued strength tends to put the onus on the doves to justify their support of the status quo, rather than on the hawks arguing for a rate rise.
"Even the middle-of-the-roaders may think it's time to take out a little (anti-inflation) insurance," a source said.
Given the internal dynamics of the Fed, any rate rise is more likely to be a quarter-percentage point than the half sought by some anti-inflation hawks, several sources suggested.
A rate increase at this time would not come at the politically most propitious time for the independent Fed, which likes to stay above the fray in an election year.

Higher rates would not be good news for President Clitnon in his race to retain the White House. But they would likely have little, if any impact, on the economy in the run-up to the November 5 election.

"This is a good time for the Fed not to make bold moves, right before an election," one central bank source said. "We do what we have to do, but if we don't have to, why not wait until after the election?"
But a growing number of Fed officials seem to be thinking that might not be the best idea.

Much of their concern has focussed on the tight labor market and fears that will lead to stepped-up wage demands and higher inflation. Average hourly earnings of workers jumped to $11.87 in August from $11.81 in July.
"The average earnings data weren't a disaster, but they were not terribly encouraging," one Fed source said.

The upward pressure on wages, including a 50-cent-an-hour increase in the government-mandated minimum wage on October 1, comes at a time when prices for food and energy are also showing signs of rising.
Oil prices shot higher this week after the United States bombed Iraq. Food prices are going up because of a poor grain harvest.
"The risks are on the side of higher inflation," one Fed source said.
"We're at a period of heightened surveillance," added another.
